description: Rhapsody in Green aims to develop a music-theoretic sonification method that translates NASA NDVI imagery into musical compositions by using the geographic distribution and geometric patterns of Earth’s vegetation to shape harmony, rhythm, and melody.
summary: Rhapsody in Green develops a music-theoretic sonification method that translates NDVI imagery featured in NASA's Earth Information Center into musical compositions. Rather than simply mapping individual data values to pitches, the method uses the geographic distribution and geometric patterns of Earth's vegetation—including geographic positions, land coverage, spatial greenness gradients, and greenness contours across geographic regions—to shape harmony, rhythm, and melody. The composition process aims to balance data fidelity and musical coherence by incorporating established music-theoretic principles, including diatonic scale structure, functional harmony, voice leading, and cadences. Applied to four seasonal NDVI images, the proposed method generates four musical compositions, presented as scores and audio clips. By transforming visual vegetation patterns into structured, musically coherent sound, Rhapsody in Green offers an alternative, multisensory way to explore Earth science beyond traditional visualizations.
details:
Introduction

The proposed sonification method translates the geographic distribution and geometric patterns of Earth's vegetation into musical compositions. It uses global Normalized Difference Vegetation Index (NDVI) imagery from NASA's SNPP Visible Infrared Imaging Radiometer Suite (VIIRS) to characterize Earth's vegetation greenness.

Sonification is performed through two complementary processes: harmony generation and melody generation. As illustrated in the figure below, each NDVI image is divided into a 32 × 16 geographic grid and separated into Northern and Southern Hemispheres, each containing 32 × 8 cells.

The method represents vegetation patterns from west to east by mapping geographic longitude to musical time across four measures in 4/4 time. Southern Hemisphere data guides harmony generation, which involves harmonic rhythm and chord progression generation. Northern Hemisphere data guides melody generation, which involves melodic rhythm and pitch contour generation. The two processes are integrated through harmonic constraints to maintain musical coherence. This architecture enables geographic and geometric vegetation features to shape different, yet interconnected, components of a unified musical composition.

Feature Extraction through Image Processing

Each NDVI image is divided into a 32 × 16 geographic grid (512 cells). Each cell spans 11.25° of longitude and latitude. Since the input images are color-coded visualizations rather than numerical NDVI datasets, pixel colors are matched to the NDVI color scale to estimate normalized greenness scores ranging from 0 to 1. Ocean, snow/ice, and pixels with excessive color mismatches are excluded from greenness estimation, while snow/ice coverage is tracked separately. For each cell, the mean and standard deviation of valid greenness scores are calculated, along with the fractions of valid greenness pixels, snow/ice, and classified land (valid pixels plus snow/ice).

To extract geographic patterns for sonification, the 32 × 16 grid is divided into Northern and Southern Hemispheres, each containing 32 × 8 cells. In each hemisphere, adjacent columns are aggregated into 8, 16, or 32 longitudinal regions, corresponding to widths of 45°, 22.5°, or 11.25°, respectively. Regional statistics are calculated using latitude-area weighting, proportional to the cosine of latitude. The resulting longitudinal profiles capture the geographic distribution of vegetation greenness and land coverage, including spatial variations and gradients. These features serve as the inputs for sonification.

Harmony Generation

Harmonic Rhythm Generation. The proposed method uses Southern Hemisphere vegetation data to generate harmonic rhythm, which determines the timing and duration of chord events. The Southern Hemisphere is initially divided into eight longitudinal regions of 45° each, with each region assigned two musical beats.

An adaptive subdivision algorithm then examines the land coverage of each region. Regions with at least 25% land coverage are subdivided into two 22.5° regions, each assigned one beat, while regions with lower land coverage retain their original two-beat duration. This process generates 8 to 16 chord events spanning 16 beats (four measures in 4/4 time). Musically, this creates a more active harmonic rhythm in land-rich regions, with more frequent chord changes, while chords are sustained longer in ocean-dominated regions. As illustrated in the left figure, this adaptive segmentation allows geographic land distribution to influence the temporal structure of harmony while maintaining a consistent west-to-east mapping of longitude to musical time.

Chord Progression Generation. Beyond harmonic rhythm, the proposed method uses the geometric patterns of Southern Hemisphere greenness to guide chord progression generation. Each longitudinal region is represented by its geographic position (longitude) and greenness. The spatial greenness gradient between successive regions is calculated as the absolute difference in greenness divided by their longitudinal separation, followed by normalization to obtain an NDVI spatial-gradient distance between 0 and 1.

To represent corresponding musical relationships, the method uses a three-pitch chord orbifold, a geometric space in which each point represents a three-note chord and distances quantify the minimum voice-leading movement between chords. Orbifold distances are calculated for six diatonic triads in a given key and normalized. The left figure shows an example orbifold for triads in C major.

The method then seeks chord progressions whose successive orbifold distances approximate the corresponding NDVI spatial-gradient distances. In this way, the geographic geometry of vegetation greenness influences the geometric relationships between successive chords.

To balance geometric representation with musical coherence, the method incorporates established principles of functional harmony into chord progression optimization. A first-order Markov model assigns transition probabilities between chords and provides a measure of harmonic plausibility.

The chord progression optimization aims to minimize a weighted objective combining geometric mismatch, calculated as the mean squared difference between NDVI and orbifold distances, and harmonic transition penalties derived from Markov probabilities. Additional constraints require the progression to begin with the tonic chord (I), establish a half cadence at the end of the second measure, and conclude with a final cadence. Candidate chord progressions are evaluated to identify solutions that balance environmental geometry with functional harmony. The left figure the objective function and an example optimization result.

Melody Generation

Melodic Rhythm Generation. The proposed method uses Northern Hemisphere vegetation data to generate melodic rhythm, which determines the timing and duration of individual notes. Like harmonic rhythm generation, the Northern Hemisphere is initially divided into eight longitudinal regions of 45° each, with each region assigned two musical beats. An adaptive rhythm generation algorithm then uses land coverage and greenness to generate half-note, quarter-note, and eighth-note patterns. Ocean-dominated regions (less than 15% land coverage) receive sustained half notes, while regions with limited land coverage or low greenness receive two quarter notes. Regions with substantial land coverage and high greenness receive four eighth notes, producing denser rhythmic patterns. For intermediate greenness levels, the algorithm generates one quarter note and two eighth notes, with their ordering determined by local variations in land coverage and greenness. The resulting melodic rhythm is aligned with the harmonic rhythm generated from Southern Hemisphere data by splitting notes at chord boundaries when necessary. This process produces a continuous melody spanning 16 beats (four measures in 4/4 time) by shaping rhythmic patterns based on the geographic distribution and greenness of Northern Hemisphere vegetation.

Pitch and Contour Generation. Beyond melodic rhythm, the method uses the magnitude and spatial variations of Northern Hemisphere greenness to guide melodic pitch selection. Each note is associated with the greenness of its corresponding longitudinal region. Greenness values are mapped to preferred pitch registers, so that higher greenness favors higher pitches. In addition to this value-based mapping, the method considers the geometric contour of greenness across successive geographic regions. Increasing greenness encourages upward melodic movement, while decreasing greenness encourages downward movement. The influence of contour matching depends on the magnitude of the greenness change; more substantial spatial variations exert a stronger influence on melodic direction. By considering not only greenness levels but also their spatial relationships, this approach allows geographic patterns of vegetation greenness to influence the melodic structure.

To balance greenness-based pitch mapping with musical coherence, the method optimizes pitch selection using three objectives: pitch register matching, melodic contour matching, and smooth melodic movement. The register error measures the deviation of a candidate pitch from the preferred pitch determined by greenness. The contour error penalizes melodic movements that conflict with the spatial direction of greenness changes, while the movement error discourages large pitch intervals between successive notes. These three errors are combined into a weighted objective function. For each melodic event, the pitch optimization process evaluates candidate pitches within the C3–B5 range, restricting them to chord tones of the underlying harmony, and selects the pitch that minimizes the combined error. The melody begins and ends on tonic notes, with an additional penalty encouraging smooth movement toward the final tonic. By combining environmental data with harmonic constraints and voice-leading principles, the resulting melody aims to capture the geographic patterns of greenness while maintaining coherence with the accompanying chord progression.

Sonified Music: A Seasonal Suite in Green

The proposed sonification method was applied to four NASA NDVI images representing different seasons: spring (May 1, 2024), summer (August 1, 2024), fall (November 1, 2024), and winter (February 1, 2025). Each image was translated into a four-measure musical composition, with harmony, rhythm, and melody shaped by the geographic distribution and geometric patterns of vegetation greenness.

Listen to summer vegetation

Listen to fall vegetation

Listen to winter vegetation

The four compositions differ in melodic rhythm, pitch register, melodic contour, and chord progression. The summer composition features the highest note density (22 notes) and a generally higher melodic register, consistent with greater Northern Hemisphere vegetation greenness. In contrast, the winter composition contains fewer notes (17) and a lower melodic register, corresponding to reduced greenness across much of the Northern Hemisphere. The spring and fall compositions exhibit intermediate note densities (19 and 20 notes, respectively), with different melodic contours and rhythmic patterns. These differences arise from the proposed method's environmental-to-musical mappings. Although all four compositions contain 11 chord events, their chord progressions differ because of variations in the underlying vegetation geometry and the resulting optimization.

Conclusion

Rhapsody in Green develops a geometry-aware sonification method that integrates the geographic distribution and geometric patterns of Earth's vegetation greenness with music-theoretic principles to generate musically coherent compositions. Rather than simply mapping individual environmental data values to musical pitches, the method uses the spatial organization of longitudinal greenness profiles to shape harmony, rhythm, and melody. Geographic longitude is mapped to musical time. Southern Hemisphere land coverage determines harmonic rhythm, while spatial greenness gradients guide chord progression optimization by matching environmental distances with chord-to-chord orbifold distances. Northern Hemisphere land coverage and greenness determine melodic rhythm, while greenness magnitudes and spatial greenness trends influence pitch registers and melodic contours. By combining these environmental features with principles of functional harmony, voice leading, and cadence formation, the proposed method aims to balance scientific data fidelity with musical coherence.

Future work will focus on evaluating the perceptual effectiveness of the proposed sonification method through listening studies. Additional experiments will study alternative geographic-to-musical mappings, including reversing the longitudinal direction (east to west), randomizing geographic sequences, and swapping the roles of the Northern and Southern Hemispheres in harmony and melody generation. Comparing these alternatives will help determine how geographic ordering, spatial relationships, and hemispheric assignments influence the recognition of vegetation patterns and musical coherence. These evaluations will provide insights into the effectiveness and potential improvements of geometry-aware sonification for environmental data.
